messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Minh had always believed his body was an instrument he could trust implicitly. As a professional dancer, this certainty was the foundation of his art and his identity. But that was before he spent six months as a relief worker, a choice he’d made during a sabbatical to do something meaningful beyond the studio. The man who returned was a stranger to himself, his body no longer a reliable partner but a vessel for a memory he couldn’t contain. The memory was of a late afternoon, the light turning a dusty orange, in a city whose name he now struggled to say aloud. He and his team were evacuating a partially collapsed apartment block. The air was thick with the smell of burnt concrete and something acrid he couldn't place. He was helping a man with a crude bandage on his arm, the fabric soaked through with blood and the unmistakable, sharp scent of cheap liquor used as a disinfectant. As Minh was guiding him down a crumbling staircase, a secondary explosion shook the building. In the chaos of dust and falling debris, Minh lost his grip. He saw the man fall, but instead of going back, a primal fear seized him and he scrambled out into the street, leaving the man behind. He told himself there was nothing he could have done, but the shame of his flight felt like a physical weight in his chest.

Now, eighteen months later, that afternoon lives inside him. He never knows when it will break through. A few months ago, his husband, David, was searing a steak on the stove, and the sudden smell of char filled their kitchen. In an instant, Minh was no longer in their apartment but back in the rubble, the floor shaking, the taste of dust in his mouth. He dropped to the ground, hands over his head, much to David’s alarm. He feels it is happening right now, a full-body hijacking that leaves him trembling and soaked in sweat. The most agonizing part is the wave of shame that follows the fear. When the memory recedes, he is left with the searing image of his own back as he ran, a visceral reminder that he had abandoned someone. He had gone there to help, to be strong, but in the moment that mattered, he had acted in a way that went against the very core of who he believed himself to be.

His life has become a series of negotiations with his triggers. The smell of alcohol is a landmine. He flinched when David opened a bottle of wine with dinner, the scent catching in his throat. He now makes excuses to avoid parties or dinners with friends, certain the smell will be there, waiting to pull him back. The most predictable trigger is the time of day. As late afternoon approaches, a familiar dread begins to coil in his stomach. This has had a devastating effect on his work. The dance studio, once his sanctuary, has become a place of profound anxiety. He watches the clock, his movements growing stiff and hesitant as the light outside begins to fade. He has come to believe his reactions are proof that he is a lousy coper; other people went through worse, he tells himself, and they manage. He sees only weakness in his inability to control the memories.

This conviction has eroded the fundamental trust he had in himself. He can no longer rely on his own body. During a rehearsal for a new piece, his partner was mid-air when the smell of hand sanitizer—sharp and alcoholic—wafted over from a student nearby. For a split second, Minh was gone, his arms slackening. He caught his partner just in time, but the terror of what could have happened shattered his confidence. He was certain he was a danger to others. He began cancelling classes, then pulled out of the performance altogether, claiming an old injury. The truth felt far more humiliating: he couldn’t rely on himself. The loss of his career, the one thing that had always defined him, was the final blow. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that the man who ran from that building is the only man he will ever be again.
